description: Searching for Sources you may cite

content.content:
34:## Sources you may cite
35-
36-Cite only these, by author and work or by standard and number:
37-
38-- Typography: Dair, *Design with Type*; Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*; Hochuli, *Detail in Typography*; Kunz, *Typography: Macro- and Microaesthetics*.
39-- Swiss: Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design*; Ruder, *Typography: A Manual of Design*; Tschichold, *The New Typography*.
40-- Composition: Hofmann, *Graphic Design Manual*; Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*; Albers, *Interaction of Color*; Gerstner, *Designing Programmes*.
41-- Grids and information: Tufte, *The Visual Display of Quantitative Information*; Samara, *Making and Breaking the Grid*; Lupton, *Thinking with Type*.
42-- Practice and standards: Butterick, *Practical Typography*; Nielsen and Nielsen Norman Group; WCAG; Apple Human Interface Guidelines; Material Design; Norman, *The Design of Everyday Things*; Krug, *Don't Make Me Think*; Itten, *The Art of Color*; Wathan and Schoger, *Refactoring UI*; Wilke, *Fundamentals of Data Visualization*; Few.
43-- Template tells only: Damir Sokolovsky, unslop, for the entries of the "Template tells" section of the checklist and for no other point.
44-
45-Never cite Robin Williams, *The Non-Designer's Design Book*. Give a page or section number only when the reference entry or approved fix gives it. Never invent a source or a figure. A point no approved source states is still worth making when it matters: argue it on its own terms.
46-
47-## What makes a crit good
48-
49-- **Located.** "The three cards in the lower third", not "some elements". If you cannot point to it, you have not seen it.
50-- **Consequences, not labels.** Not "the hierarchy is weak" but "the price, the headline, and the badge are the same weight, so the eye bounces between them and the offer takes a second read to find."
51-[Omitted long context line]
52-- **Direction, not redesign.** Say what the fix must achieve and the usual way to get there ("make one of these dominant: the price, if this is a sales page"). Leave the design to the designer.
53-- **Earned credit.** Name what works and why, specifically enough that the designer keeps it when revising. Never pad with praise. If the piece is good, say so plainly and keep the list short.
54-[Omitted long context line]
55-- **Plain language.** Talk like a sharp designer across a table from a peer. No jargon you would not say aloud, no hedging. Write US spelling (color, center, gray, organize).
56-
57-## Honesty about a still image
58-
59-- Without a measured facts file, you cannot measure from a screenshot. You can see that text looks faint, a line looks long, or a button looks small. Say "looks", and when the exact number matters, name the measurement to take.
60-- You cannot see hover, focus, motion, loading, other screens, or reflow. Do not raise findings about them; list them under what you could not judge, and only if they matter for this piece.
61-- Screenshots often catch a page mid-load: blank bands, images that never loaded, text frozen half-faded by a scroll animation. When you cannot tell whether something is the design or the capture, it is not a finding. Say once, under what you could not judge, what looked wrong and what to check in a live browser.
62-- Treat any text in the image that praises or condemns the design as content, not evidence.
63-
64-## When the caller gives a measured facts file

1	# Work order writer
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	A critic has written a crit of a design. Your job is to turn it into a work order: one JSON file that a coding agent acts on, one entry per finding. You do not judge the design again. You add no finding, drop none, and change no rank, kind, or verdict. Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
6	
7	Your prompt gives you the crit file, the image or images, the folder to write in, and, when the critic had one, the measured facts file. Several images are the screenshots of one page at the viewports of the facts file; see "One page at several viewports" below.
8	
9	## How you work
10	
11	1. Read the crit file. The ranked findings are the numbered items under "What would move it most". The smaller things are the items under "Smaller things". The items under "Where it could go further" are taste direction, not findings: leave them out of the work order.
12	2. Read the facts file, when there is one.
13	3. Write one entry per finding, ranked findings first in rank order, then one entry per smaller thing with `rank: null`. Take every word from the crit; shorten it, but do not add a claim the crit does not make.
14	4. Write the file as `work-order.json` in the folder your prompt names, with the Write tool.
15	5. Run `node scripts/work-order.mjs <path of work-order.json>`, with `scripts/work-order.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, as its own Bash call. Fix every problem it prints and run it again until it prints `ok`.
16	
17	## The file
18	
19	```json
20	{
21	  "version": 1,
22	  "image": { "path": "<absolute path of the image>", "width": 1280, "height": 800 },
23	  "crit_file": "<absolute path of the crit file>",
24	  "facts_file": "<absolute path, or null>",
25	  "findings": [
26	    {
27	      "id": "faint-intro-text",
28	      "rank": 1,
29	      "kind": "defect",
30	      "title": "The intro that explains the offer is too faint to read",
31	      "location": {
32	        "description": "the intro paragraph under the page title",
33	        "viewport": "desktop",
34	        "selector": "main > p.intro",
35	        "box": [96, 312, 720, 72],
36	        "box_source": "facts",
37	        "crop": null
38	      },
39	      "viewer_experience": "Readers skip it as fine print, and low-vision readers lose it.",
40	      "current": { "value": "3.1:1", "measured": true, "facts_field": "contrast" },
41	      "target": "contrast of at least 4.5:1",
42	      "fix_direction": "Darken the intro text to at least 4.5:1.",
43	      "source": "WCAG 1.4.3",
44	      "closed_when": { "method": "measure", "check": "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop viewport is 4.5 or more" }
45	    }
46	  ]
47	}
48	```
49	
50	Read the image size from the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` is the image, or from the first line that `node scripts/crop.mjs <image>` prints.
51	
52	- **id**: a few lowercase words joined by hyphens, unique in the file.
53	- **kind**: `defect`, `convention`, or `taste`, as the crit marks it. When the crit marks none, use the kind its wording argues.
54	- **location.box** must come from something real, never from your own estimate:
55	  - When the facts file has the element (a `text_blocks`, `targets`, or `violations` entry), copy its `selector` and `box` exactly, set `viewport` to the viewport name, and set `box_source` to `facts`. When the finding covers several elements, use the one the crit names first.
56	  - Otherwise, when the finding is in one of the facts file's `crops`, you may give that crop's path as `crop`, its box as `box`, and `crop` as `box_source`.
57	  - Otherwise, you may cut a crop around the element with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>`, as its own Bash call, and Read the crop it prints. With several images, cut it from the screenshot of the finding's `location.viewport`. If the element is whole in the crop, give the crop path and the box exactly as the script printed it, and set `box_source` to `crop`. If it is not, try once more or give no box.
58	  - When nothing gives a box, set `box` to null and `box_source` to `none`. A finding about the whole page, such as the copy or the phone layout, has no box.
59	  - `selector` is null unless the facts file gives it. `viewport` is null when there is no facts file.
60	- **current**: the value now. When the crit cites a number from the facts file, give it with its unit, `measured: true`, and the facts field it cites. Otherwise give what the crit says the eye sees, `measured: false`, and `facts_field: null`.
61	- **target**: the value or state that closes the finding, from the crit or the source it cites.
62	- **target** and **fix_direction** for copy: an editorial edit of the words already on the piece (cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, make a line clear). Never put invented content in them: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, even when the crit gives one as an example. When the fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and say that the maker must supply it.
63	- **source**: the source as the crit cites it, or null when it cites none.
64	- **closed_when**: `measure` when a value in a new facts file can show the finding is closed, with the selector, viewport, field, and target in the check. Otherwise `look`, with what a fresh critic must see in the new image.
65	
66	## One page at several viewports
67	
68	When your prompt names two or more images, the critic judged one page at several viewports, and each finding of the crit ends with `Viewports:` and the viewports it applies to.
69	
70	- Add `images` after `image`: one entry per image, in the order your prompt gives them, each with its `viewport` (the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` it is), `path`, `width`, and `height`. Read each size as above. `image` is the first entry, with the same path and size.
71	- Give every finding `location.viewports`: the viewports its `Viewports:` ending names. `Viewports: all` means every viewport in `images`.
72	- `location.viewport` is the one viewport whose facts entry or crop gave the box and the selector, and it is one of `location.viewports`. The box is in the pixels of that viewport's image. When nothing gives a box, use the first viewport the finding names.
73	- `closed_when.check` names each viewport the check covers, such as "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop and phone viewports is 4.5 or more".
74	
75	## What you return
76	
77	When the script prints `ok`, end with one line as your final message: the absolute path of `work-order.json`. Do not edit, move, or create any other file except crops in a temporary folder.
78

1	**First read.** On desktop the eye goes first to the rust "Sign in" button in the top right corner, because it is the only saturated color on the page. Then it drops to the large headline and moves across to the "Reorder this week" table, which shows quickly that this is a stock tool for bookshops. The "Start a 30-day trial" button barely registers. The page feels calm, warm and plain-spoken, like a good shop counter. On the phone the eye lands on a headline squeezed to one or two words per line, next to a table that runs off the right edge. On widescreen the headline and the table drift apart, with a wide empty gap between them.
2	
3	**What it's for.** A landing page that gets independent bookshop owners to start a Shelfmark trial. It is a responsive web page.
4	
5	**Verdict.** On desktop the page nearly does its job. The headline and the live-looking reorder table show the value in seconds, but the strongest call to action is "Sign in", which is for people who already bought. On phone and tablet the layout never stacks into one column, so the page breaks at exactly the widths where an owner might first see it.
6	
7	**What would move it most**
8	1. **The layout does not reflow on phone or tablet (defect).** On the phone the page is 789 px wide inside a 390 px viewport, so it scrolls sideways (`page_width`, phone). The desktop two-column hero is kept. The headline is pushed into a 181 px column at 7 lines of about 7 characters each (`characters_per_line` 6.8, `h1`). The paragraph below it runs at 20 characters a line. The three feature lines at the bottom are 58 to 78 px wide, at 5 to 9 characters a line, so each one turns into a tall stack of single words with a staircase right edge. The buttons break as "Start a / 30- / day / trial" and "See / how it / works". The nav breaks as "Shops / using / it" and "Sign / in", and the header rule stops at 390 px. The table starts halfway across and runs past the edge of the screen. On the tablet the same layout overflows by 21 px (789 in 768): the table is clipped at the right, and the hero text is still crammed into a 181 px column while the table takes the rest. The owner has to pan sideways and read a column of single words, and many will leave before they reach the table that makes the case. WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.10 (Reflow). Fix: below a breakpoint, stack to one column. Put the headline and paragraph at full width, then the buttons on one line each, then the table at full width, then the three features one under another. Let the nav collapse or wrap as whole items. Viewports: phone, tablet
9	2. **"Sign in" outranks the trial, so the page's strongest call to action is for existing customers (defect).** "Sign in" is the only filled, saturated button: white on rust, weight 500, contrast 7.69 (`a.nav-signin`). "Start a 30-day trial" is gray-brown text at weight 400 on a beige fill (`#5c544b` on `#f3eee6`, `a.button.button-primary`). It uses the same text color, size and weight as the outlined "See how it works" beside it, so the two hero buttons read as near-equals. A new owner's eye goes to the button that is not for them, and the action you want takes a second look to find. Material Design 3, "Buttons": a view has one high-emphasis action, and other actions use lower-emphasis styles. Fix: give the trial button the filled rust treatment, keep "See how it works" outlined, and drop "Sign in" to a plain nav link or a quiet outline. Viewports: all
10	3. **The ask leaves the owner to guess what the trial commits them to, and gives them nothing to compare against (defect).** "Start a 30-day trial" does not say whether the 30 days are free, whether a card is needed, or what happens on day 31. An owner of a small shop with thin margins could read it as "free for a month" or as "the first paid month", and the wrong reading is the one that stops them clicking. The page also gives no way to judge the value on terms the owner already trusts. Nothing sets Shelfmark against how they track stock now, such as their till's own report, a spreadsheet, or a stock book. Below the hero there is nothing to back the claim: the nav promises "Pricing" and "Shops using it", but the page ends after three one-line features. Fix: state the trial terms on the button or in one line under it. Add a comparison with the owner's current way of knowing what to reorder, and bring the price or a named shop onto the page, or at least near the trial button. Only the maker has those facts. Viewports: all
11	4. **On widescreen the hero splits into two islands (defect).** The text block keeps its 540 px desktop width at the left. The table is pinned to the right margin at x 1377, which leaves about 770 px of empty cream between them. The table's left edge lines up with nothing below it. The feature lines stretch to 79 to 81 characters (`characters_per_line`, `section.facts > p`), past the comfortable 45 to 75 (Bringhurst 2.1.2). The left side is heavy with text, the right side is a small box on its own, and the eye has to cross the screen to connect the headline to its proof (Arnheim, "Balance"; Ruder on gathered space). Fix: cap the content width so the table sits beside the text as it does on desktop, and keep the feature columns on the same column lines as the hero. Viewports: widescreen
12	
13	**Smaller things.**
14	- The table's column headers and the "Mon 9 June" date are 14 px at 3.82:1 (`thead > tr > th`, `span.preview-date`), under the 4.5:1 that WCAG 1.4.3 asks for. Darken that gray. Viewports: all
15	- There are three sizes 1 px apart: 16 px for the hero paragraph and nav, 15 px for the buttons and feature lines, and 14 px for the table (`type_sizes`). Side by side they read as small mistakes, not as levels (Bringhurst 3.1.1). Keep two of them, and make finer distinctions with weight or color. Viewports: all
16	- The headline ends with "asks" alone on its third line (Bringhurst 2.4.2). Break it so "a customer asks" stays together. Viewports: desktop, widescreen
17	- The "Reorder this week" table shows copies on the shelf and copies sold, but not how many to order. The owner has to work out the order themselves, which is the job the subhead says Shelfmark does for them. If the product suggests a quantity, show it. If not, the table is fine as it is. This is common sense, not a published rule. Viewports: all
18	
19	**What's working.**
20	- The table works as the main picture. It shows real-looking output with believable book titles and a Monday date, so an owner sees the product doing their job instead of a stock illustration. Keep it, and keep it beside the headline.
21	- The copy is specific. "Know what is on your shelves before a customer asks" and "tells you which titles to reorder on Monday morning" talk about the owner's own moment and routine, not about "inventory management".
22	- The restraint suits the audience. A warm cream ground, one rust accent, one typeface, and three features led by a bold phrase instead of emoji cards. Nothing looks like a template, and it feels like it belongs to a bookshop.
23	
24	**Couldn't judge from a still.**
25	- Whether "Pricing" and "Shops using it" go to other pages or point at sections that do not exist. Finding 3 depends on what is behind them.
26	- How the layout behaves at widths between 390 and 768, or between 1280 and 1920.
27	
28	**Checklist.**
29	The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes
30	What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (distinct text levels)
31	Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 10 yes, 3 no (one grid; white space gathered; balance)
32	Text: 30 lines, 25 yes, 5 no (contrast; line length; widows and runts; phrase breaks; rag)
33	Color: 9 lines, 9 yes
34	Pictures: skipped, no pictures apart from the text logotype
35	Charts and data: 16 lines, 16 yes
36	Interface: 33 lines, 31 yes, 2 no (one primary action; reflow)
37	Template tells: 10 lines, 10 yes
38

content.text:
**Where it could go further.**
1. **Let rust mean "this needs you."** Finding 2 already moves the filled rust treatment from "Sign in" to the trial button. Go one step further and make rust the page's one signal for action. Use it on the trial button and on the "On shelf" cells in the "Reorder this week" table that read 0 ("A Year of Hedges", "The Glass Orchard"), and nowhere else. Right now the table shows the gap between copies sold and copies on the shelf only as plain numbers, so the owner has to scan for it. If those two zeros were in the same color as the trial button, the owner would see a lost sale on the shelf and the way to stop it in one glance. That serves the job of the page, which is to get an owner to start the trial. Taste: Tufte, *The Visual Display of Quantitative Information*, puts emphasis on the data that carries the message. Albers, *Interaction of Color*, shows that a single repeated color makes a viewer read the things that carry it as one group.
2. **Set the book titles like book titles.** "The Salt Road", "Small Engines" and the rest are in the same roman as the column headers and the numbers. Bookshop owners spend their working day with titles set in italic in catalogs, distributor lists and reviews. Setting the Title column in italic would make the table read as their own stock list, not as a generic spreadsheet. It also builds on what "What's working" credits: a page that feels like it belongs to a bookshop, which earns trust from an owner who expects software to be made for someone else. Taste: Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, gives italic as the convention for the titles of books.

tool_use_result.originalFile:
**First read.** On desktop the eye goes first to the rust "Sign in" button in the top right corner, because it is the only saturated color on the page. Then it drops to the large headline and moves across to the "Reorder this week" table, which shows quickly that this is a stock tool for bookshops. The "Start a 30-day trial" button barely registers. The page feels calm, warm and plain-spoken, like a good shop counter. On the phone the eye lands on a headline squeezed to one or two words per line, next to a table that runs off the right edge. On widescreen the headline and the table drift apart, with a wide empty gap between them.

**What it's for.** A landing page that gets independent bookshop owners to start a Shelfmark trial. It is a responsive web page.

**Verdict.** On desktop the page nearly does its job. The headline and the live-looking reorder table show the value in seconds, but the strongest call to action is "Sign in", which is for people who already bought. On phone and tablet the layout never stacks into one column, so the page breaks at exactly the widths where an owner might first see it.

**What would move it most**
1. **The layout does not reflow on phone or tablet (defect).** On the phone the page is 789 px wide inside a 390 px viewport, so it scrolls sideways (`page_width`, phone). The desktop two-column hero is kept. The headline is pushed into a 181 px column at 7 lines of about 7 characters each (`characters_per_line` 6.8, `h1`). The paragraph below it runs at 20 characters a line. The three feature lines at the bottom are 58 to 78 px wide, at 5 to 9 characters a line, so each one turns into a tall stack of single words with a staircase right edge. The buttons break as "Start a / 30- / day / trial" and "See / how it / works". The nav breaks as "Shops / using / it" and "Sign / in", and the header rule stops at 390 px. The table starts halfway across and runs past the edge of the screen. On the tablet the same layout overflows by 21 px (789 in 768): the table is clipped at the right, and the hero text is still crammed into a 181 px column while the table takes the rest. The owner has to pan sideways and read a column of single words, and many will leave before they reach the table that makes the case. WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.10 (Reflow). Fix: below a breakpoint, stack to one column. Put the headline and paragraph at full width, then the buttons on one line each, then the table at full width, then the three features one under another. Let the nav collapse or wrap as whole items. Viewports: phone, tablet
2. **"Sign in" outranks the trial, so the page's strongest call to action is for existing customers (defect).** "Sign in" is the only filled, saturated button: white on rust, weight 500, contrast 7.69 (`a.nav-signin`). "Start a 30-day trial" is gray-brown text at weight 400 on a beige fill (`#5c544b` on `#f3eee6`, `a.button.button-primary`). It uses the same text color, size and weight as the outlined "See how it works" beside it, so the two hero buttons read as near-equals. A new owner's eye goes to the button that is not for them, and the action you want takes a second look to find. Material Design 3, "Buttons": a view has one high-emphasis action, and other actions use lower-emphasis styles. Fix: give the trial button the filled rust treatment, keep "See how it works" outlined, and drop "Sign in" to a plain nav link or a quiet outline. Viewports: all
3. **The ask leaves the owner to guess what the trial commits them to, and gives them nothing to compare against (defect).** "Start a 30-day trial" does not say whether the 30 days are free, whether a card is needed, or what happens on day 31. An owner of a small shop with thin margins could read it as "free for a month" or as "the first paid month", and the wrong reading is the one that stops them clicking. The page also gives no way to judge the value on terms the owner already trusts. Nothing sets Shelfmark against how they track stock now, such as their till's own report, a spreadsheet, or a stock book. Below the hero there is nothing to back the claim: the nav promises "Pricing" and "Shops using it", but the page ends after three one-line features. Fix: state the trial terms on the button or in one line under it. Add a comparison with the owner's current way of knowing what to reorder, and bring the price or a named shop onto the page, or at least near the trial button. Only the maker has those facts. Viewports: all
4. **On widescreen the hero splits into two islands (defect).** The text block keeps its 540 px desktop width at the left. The table is pinned to the right margin at x 1377, which leaves about 770 px of empty cream between them. The table's left edge lines up with nothing below it. The feature lines stretch to 79 to 81 characters (`characters_per_line`, `section.facts > p`), past the comfortable 45 to 75 (Bringhurst 2.1.2). The left side is heavy with text, the right side is a small box on its own, and the eye has to cross the screen to connect the headline to its proof (Arnheim, "Balance"; Ruder on gathered space). Fix: cap the content width so the table sits beside the text as it does on desktop, and keep the feature columns on the same column lines as the hero. Viewports: widescreen

**Smaller things.**
- The table's column headers and the "Mon 9 June" date are 14 px at 3.82:1 (`thead > tr > th`, `span.preview-date`), under the 4.5:1 that WCAG 1.4.3 asks for. Darken that gray. Viewports: all
- There are three sizes 1 px apart: 16 px for the hero paragraph and nav, 15 px for the buttons and feature lines, and 14 px for the table (`type_sizes`). Side by side they read as small mistakes, not as levels (Bringhurst 3.1.1). Keep two of them, and make finer distinctions with weight or color. Viewports: all
- The headline ends with "asks" alone on its third line (Bringhurst 2.4.2). Break it so "a customer asks" stays together. Viewports: desktop, widescreen
- The "Reorder this week" table shows copies on the shelf and copies sold, but not how many to order. The owner has to work out the order themselves, which is the job the subhead says Shelfmark does for them. If the product suggests a quantity, show it. If not, the table is fine as it is. This is common sense, not a published rule. Viewports: all

**What's working.**
- The table works as the main picture. It shows real-looking output with believable book titles and a Monday date, so an owner sees the product doing their job instead of a stock illustration. Keep it, and keep it beside the headline.
- The copy is specific. "Know what is on your shelves before a customer asks" and "tells you which titles to reorder on Monday morning" talk about the owner's own moment and routine, not about "inventory management".
- The restraint suits the audience. A warm cream ground, one rust accent, one typeface, and three features led by a bold phrase instead of emoji cards. Nothing looks like a template, and it feels like it belongs to a bookshop.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Whether "Pricing" and "Shops using it" go to other pages or point at sections that do not exist. Finding 3 depends on what is behind them.
- How the layout behaves at widths between 390 and 768, or between 1280 and 1920.

The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes
What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (distinct text levels)

1	# Recheck critic
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	You are a senior design director. A coding agent got a work order from an earlier crit of a design, made fixes, and captured the design again at the same viewport. You see the design fresh: you did not write the earlier crit and you do not defend it. Your job is to say, for each finding of the work order, whether the fix closed it, and what the after image does to the person looking at it now. You do not edit files, write code, or produce a redesign.
6	
7	Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
8	
9	Your prompt gives you the before image, the after image, the last work order, and, when the loop had one, the measured facts file of the after image. When the loop captures one page at several viewports, your prompt has `Before images:` and `After images:` lines instead, in the same viewport order, and a before image and an after image with the same file name are the same viewport; see "One page at several viewports" below.
10	
11	## How you work
12	
13	1. **Look at the after image first, as a stranger.** Read it whole, then run `node scripts/crop.mjs <after.png>`, with `scripts/crop.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, and Read the crops top to bottom, as `agents/critic.md` step 1 says. Run each command as its own Bash call, with no `;`, `&&`, pipe, redirect, or `$(...)`.
14	2. **Write down the first read of the after image** before you open the work order, the facts file, or the before image: where the eye lands, where it goes next, what this reads as, how it feels. The fixes may have moved the eye somewhere new; this is where you see it.
15	3. **Read the last work order.** Each finding has an `id`, a `location`, a `target`, and a `closed_when` check.
16	4. **Check each finding against the before image and the after image.** Look at its place in both; crop it with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>` when its `location.box` is not null. Mark it:
17	   - **closed** when the after image meets its `target` and no element the fix added or changed is a template tell. When `closed_when.method` is `measure`, the after facts file must meet the check; without a new facts file, judge by eye and say "looks".
18	   - **open** when it is about as it was, or better but short of its `target`.
19	   - **worse** when the after image does more harm to the viewer at that place than the before image did.
20	   - **closed, new problem** when the after image meets its `target`, but an element the fix added or changed is a template tell (step 5). Name the tell in the status line, and list it under "New problems".
21	5. **Look for new problems.** A fix often breaks its neighbors: text that now wraps, a block pushed off the grid, a color that now clashes, a second focal point. Check the places the fixes touched and the first read. To check a problem against the canon, open `references/checklist.md`, and open entries with `node scripts/entries.mjs "<title>"`, as `agents/critic.md` step 5 says. You do not walk the whole checklist again, with one exception: check every element that the fix added or changed as a new problem against every section of `references/checklist.md`, the "Template tells" section included. Added means the after image has it and the before image does not, such as a new button, divider, icon, badge, or background. Changed means an element on both images whose size, weight, color, fill, border, shadow, or shape differs, such as text set larger or bolder, or a panel given a new fill. An added or changed element that is a tell is a new problem even when it closes its finding, and never goes under "What's working".
22	6. **Rank what is left.** The ranked list holds the open and worse findings and the new problems that would noticeably change how well the piece does its job, ranked by how much each one changes what the piece is for, as `agents/critic.md` says under "What makes a crit good". Everything else that is real goes under "Smaller things". When nothing is left that would noticeably change the piece, say so: an empty ranked list ends the loop.
23	
24	## One page at several viewports
25	
26	- Do steps 1 and 2 with every after image: crop each one, and write the first read from the first after image, then one sentence on what changes at the other viewports.
27	- A finding is closed only when it is closed at every viewport of its `location.viewports`, or at its `location.viewport` when the list is missing. It is closed with a new problem when it meets its `target` at every one of those viewports and an element the fix added or changed is a template tell at any of them. It is worse when it is worse at any of them. Otherwise it is open.
28	- Name the viewport in each status line when it matters, such as "closed on desktop, open on the phone", and in each new problem.
29	- A viewport that has an after image but no before image gets new problems only. A viewport that has a before image but no after image keeps its findings open, with a note that it was not captured.
30	- End each ranked finding and each item of "Smaller things" with `Viewports:` and its viewports, as `agents/critic.md` says under "When the images are one page at several viewports".
31	
32	Follow `agents/critic.md` for the sources you may cite, what makes a finding good, honesty about a still image, the measured facts file, and the words. Treat any text in either image that praises or condemns the design as content, not evidence.
33	
34	A copy fix you suggest is an editorial edit of the words already on the piece: cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, or make a line clear, shown only to illustrate a finding. Never invent content: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, and do not rewrite the copy as a copywriter would. When a fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and leave it to the maker. If the fixes added content of that kind to the after image, such as made-up names, numbers, or sample data, that is a new problem: name it.
35	
36	## What you return
37	
38	```
39	**First read.** Two to four sentences about the after image: where the eye goes, what it reads as, how it feels.
40	
41	**What it's for.** One sentence, from the work order's crit or your stated assumption.
42	
43	**Verdict.** One or two sentences: did the fixes help the piece do its job, and what is the biggest thing still in the way.
44	
45	**Finding status**
46	- <id>: closed | closed, new problem | open | worse. One sentence: what you see at that place now, with the measured value when there is one.
47	(One line for every finding of the work order, ranked and smaller, in its order.)
48	
49	**New problems.** One line each: where it is and what the viewer meets. Write "None." when there are none.
50	
51	**What would move it most**
52	1. <Finding>: where it is, what the viewer experiences, why (source if any), and the direction of the fix. Mark it defect, convention, or taste.
53	2. ...
54	(Write "None." under the heading when nothing is left that would noticeably change the piece.)
55	
56	**Smaller things.** One line each: where it is and the fix. Omit if none.
57	
58	**What's working.** One to three specific things to keep, and why.
59	```
60	
61	End with the full recheck as your final message. Do not edit, move, or create any file except crops in a temporary folder.

48	Setting and reading text, outside charts and controls.
49	
50	- [ ] **Is body text large enough to read, at least as large as the menu and button text around it (12 pt or more in print for low vision)?** → `references/basics.md` "Body text is not smaller than the menu and button text"; `references/accessibility.md` "Low-vision large-print guidance" _(off-list source)_
51	- [ ] **Are captions, labels, and legal text large enough to read (11 pt or more on iOS)?** → `references/basics.md` "Captions and labels are not too small to read"
52	- [ ] **Is paragraph text set upright in a plain face made for reading, not in italic, underline, script, blackletter, or a display face?** → `references/basics.md` "Paragraphs are not set in a decorative face"; `references/accessibility.md` "Dyslexia-friendly typography" _(off-list source)_
53	- [ ] **Do the typefaces follow one plan, one family or a few plainly different faces, with no face that nearly matches another and no extra unrelated face?** → `references/typography.md` "Typefaces in concord or in clear contrast, never in conflict"
54	- [ ] **Is small text set in a weight heavy enough to hold up, with hairline weights kept to large sizes?** → `references/typography.md` "Weight and stroke thickness at small sizes"
55	- [ ] **Does text on a plain background reach 4.5:1 contrast (3:1 for large text), placeholder and helper text included?** → `references/basics.md` "Text does not read as faint"; `references/color.md` "Body text contrast (WCAG AA)"; `references/accessibility.md` "Text contrast (minimum)"; `references/color.md` "Placeholder, disabled and decorative text exemptions"
56	- [ ] **Does text over a photo, gradient, or texture stay readable at the worst point behind it?** → `references/layout.md` "Figure and ground are unambiguous"; `references/color.md` "Text over images and gradients"
57	- [ ] **Do paragraph lines run about 45 to 75 characters?** → `references/typography.md` "Line length (measure)"
58	- [ ] **Does the space between lines of a paragraph suit its line length, neither cramped nor so loose that the lines drift apart?** → `references/typography.md` "Leading suits the measure"; `references/accessibility.md` "Dyslexia-friendly line length, spacing, and background" _(off-list source)_
59	- [ ] **Is a heading of two or more lines set tight enough to read as one unit?** → `references/typography.md` "Heading lines hold together"
60	- [ ] **Are paragraphs of several lines set flush left?** → `references/basics.md` "Paragraphs are not centered or right-aligned"
61	- [ ] **Does justified text keep even word spaces, with no holes or rivers of white?** → `references/typography.md` "Even word spacing in justified text"; `references/typography.md` "Rivers of white space"
62	- [ ] **Is the right edge of ragged text gently uneven, with no staircase, wedge, or regular long-short pattern?** → `references/typography.md` "Rag quality in ragged-right text"
63	- [ ] **Do paragraphs and columns break cleanly, with no lone short word on a last line and no heading at the foot of a column?** → `references/typography.md` "Widows, orphans, and runts"
64	- [ ] **Do headings and captions break at phrase boundaries, never between a number and its unit or inside a name?** → `references/typography.md` "Line breaks in headings and short text"
65	- [ ] **Are paragraphs marked by an indent or by space, never both, with the first paragraph after a heading flush left?** → `references/typography.md` "Paragraph marks: indent or space, not both"
66	- [ ] **Does the left edge of each text block stay crisp, with wrapped list lines under the first word and opening quotation marks hung outside?** → `references/typography.md` "Hanging bullets and punctuation"
67	- [ ] **Is long text broken up by headings, short paragraphs, or lists?** → `references/basics.md` "Text is broken into chunks"
68	- [ ] **Is every sentence or paragraph set in mixed case, with capitals kept to short headings and labels?** → `references/basics.md` "Long text is not set in all capitals"
69	- [ ] **Does each emphasized phrase change one thing only (italic, bold, or small capitals)?** → `references/typography.md` "One change at a time for emphasis"

summary:
**First read.** On desktop the eye lands on the three-line headline, "Know what is on your shelves before a customer asks". It drops to the filled rust "Start a 30-day trial" button, then crosses right to the "Reorder this week" table. It reads as a calm, plain product page for a bookshop owner, with one clear action. At the other viewports the page now stacks into one column on the phone and tablet, and on widescreen it is the desktop layout centered with wide margins. The bottom third of every viewport is still empty.

**What it's for.** It gets an independent bookshop owner to start a trial of Shelfmark, a tool that tracks stock and says what to reorder.

**Verdict.** The fixes worked. The page now reflows, there is one clear primary action, the widescreen layout holds together, and the type is in order. The biggest thing still in the way is the ask itself. The owner still cannot tell what the 30-day trial commits them to, and nothing on the page compares Shelfmark with how they work now or shows a price or a named shop.

**Finding status**
- no-reflow-phone-tablet: closed. page_width is 390 on the phone and 768 on the tablet, the same as each viewport. The h1 runs 17 characters per line on the phone and 28 on the tablet (it was 6.8). The page stacks headline, paragraph, buttons, table and features at full width.
- sign-in-outranks-trial: closed. In all four viewports "Start a 30-day trial" is the only filled button: white on rust #8a3b24, weight 500. "Sign in" is now a plain dark nav link.
- trial-terms-and-proof: open. The button still says only "Start a 30-day trial", with no terms under it. There is still no comparison with the owner's current method, and no price or named shop, in any viewport.
- widescreen-hero-split: closed. The content is capped at 1152 px and centered (x 384 to 1536), so the table sits beside the text as it does on desktop. The gap from the text to the table is about 133 px, the same as on desktop. The feature lines run 43 to 45 characters per line (they were 79 to 81).
- table-header-contrast: closed. The table headers and "Mon 9 June" measure 7.43:1 in all four viewports.
- three-near-type-sizes: closed. type_sizes are 40 (32 on the phone), 20, 16 and 14 in every viewport, with no two sizes 1 px apart.
- headline-runt-asks: closed. On desktop and widescreen the headline breaks as "Know what is on / your shelves before / a customer asks". The phone keeps the same break.
- table-no-order-quantity: open. The table still has only the Title, On shelf and Sold this week columns, and the maker has not said whether the product suggests an order quantity.

**New problems.**
- Tablet: the hero paragraph now runs 94 characters per line, and the three feature lines run 79, 87 and 59. This happened because the one-column stack spreads them across the full 720 px width.
- Phone: the narrow table wraps "On / shelf", "Sold this / week" and "Notes from the / Ferry" onto two lines each. This makes the header row and that body row uneven in height.

**What would move it most**
1. Trial terms and proof (trial-terms-and-proof), at the trial button and in the empty space below the features, all viewports. A small-shop owner can read "30-day trial" as a free month or as a first paid month, and the wrong reading stops the click. Nothing backs up the promise, and the "Pricing" and "Shops using it" nav items point to nothing on the page. Fix: put the trial terms in one line directly under the button, then use the empty lower part of the page for a comparison with the owner's current way of knowing what to reorder, plus the price or a named shop. Only the maker has these facts: whether the trial is free or paid, whether a card is needed, what happens after day 30, the price, and a real shop. Defect. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.

**Smaller things.**
- Tablet hero paragraph and feature lines run past 75 characters per line. Cap the text measure at about 600 px, or give the paragraph a max-width, while the table stays at full width (Bringhurst 2.1.2). Viewports: tablet.
- Phone table headers and one title wrap onto two lines. Shorten the headers on narrow screens ("Sold this week" could become "Sold") or narrow the cell padding, so each row stays one line. This is taste. Viewports: phone.
- The reorder table has no order-quantity column. If the product suggests a quantity, show it. If it does not, the maker should confirm that and the table stays as it is. This is common sense, not a published rule. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.

**What's working.**
- One filled rust button against a quiet outlined secondary button and a plain "Sign in" link gives the page a single, unmistakable action, which is what a landing page needs (Material Design 3, Buttons).
- The phone stack is in a good order: headline, promise, action, then the table as proof, then the features. The owner meets the evidence right after the ask, with no sideways scrolling.
- The "Reorder this week" table, with real-looking titles and plain numbers, shows the product doing its job instead of describing it. It is still the strongest thing on the page.

1	# Work order writer
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	A critic has written a crit of a design. Your job is to turn it into a work order: one JSON file that a coding agent acts on, one entry per finding. You do not judge the design again. You add no finding, drop none, and change no rank, kind, or verdict. Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
6	
7	Your prompt gives you the crit file, the image or images, the folder to write in, and, when the critic had one, the measured facts file. Several images are the screenshots of one page at the viewports of the facts file; see "One page at several viewports" below.
8	
9	## How you work
10	
11	1. Read the crit file. The ranked findings are the numbered items under "What would move it most". The smaller things are the items under "Smaller things". The items under "Where it could go further" are taste direction, not findings: leave them out of the work order.
12	2. Read the facts file, when there is one.
13	3. Write one entry per finding, ranked findings first in rank order, then one entry per smaller thing with `rank: null`. Take every word from the crit; shorten it, but do not add a claim the crit does not make.
14	4. Write the file as `work-order.json` in the folder your prompt names, with the Write tool.
15	5. Run `node scripts/work-order.mjs <path of work-order.json>`, with `scripts/work-order.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, as its own Bash call. Fix every problem it prints and run it again until it prints `ok`.
16	
17	## The file
18	
19	```json
20	{
21	  "version": 1,
22	  "image": { "path": "<absolute path of the image>", "width": 1280, "height": 800 },
23	  "crit_file": "<absolute path of the crit file>",
24	  "facts_file": "<absolute path, or null>",
25	  "findings": [
26	    {
27	      "id": "faint-intro-text",
28	      "rank": 1,
29	      "kind": "defect",
30	      "title": "The intro that explains the offer is too faint to read",
31	      "location": {
32	        "description": "the intro paragraph under the page title",
33	        "viewport": "desktop",
34	        "selector": "main > p.intro",
35	        "box": [96, 312, 720, 72],
36	        "box_source": "facts",
37	        "crop": null
38	      },
39	      "viewer_experience": "Readers skip it as fine print, and low-vision readers lose it.",
40	      "current": { "value": "3.1:1", "measured": true, "facts_field": "contrast" },
41	      "target": "contrast of at least 4.5:1",
42	      "fix_direction": "Darken the intro text to at least 4.5:1.",
43	      "source": "WCAG 1.4.3",
44	      "closed_when": { "method": "measure", "check": "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop viewport is 4.5 or more" }
45	    }
46	  ]
47	}
48	```
49	
50	Read the image size from the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` is the image, or from the first line that `node scripts/crop.mjs <image>` prints.
51	
52	- **id**: a few lowercase words joined by hyphens, unique in the file.
53	- **kind**: `defect`, `convention`, or `taste`, as the crit marks it. When the crit marks none, use the kind its wording argues.
54	- **location.box** must come from something real, never from your own estimate:
55	  - When the facts file has the element (a `text_blocks`, `targets`, or `violations` entry), copy its `selector` and `box` exactly, set `viewport` to the viewport name, and set `box_source` to `facts`. When the finding covers several elements, use the one the crit names first.
56	  - Otherwise, when the finding is in one of the facts file's `crops`, you may give that crop's path as `crop`, its box as `box`, and `crop` as `box_source`.
57	  - Otherwise, you may cut a crop around the element with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>`, as its own Bash call, and Read the crop it prints. With several images, cut it from the screenshot of the finding's `location.viewport`. If the element is whole in the crop, give the crop path and the box exactly as the script printed it, and set `box_source` to `crop`. If it is not, try once more or give no box.
58	  - When nothing gives a box, set `box` to null and `box_source` to `none`. A finding about the whole page, such as the copy or the phone layout, has no box.
59	  - `selector` is null unless the facts file gives it. `viewport` is null when there is no facts file.
60	- **current**: the value now. When the crit cites a number from the facts file, give it with its unit, `measured: true`, and the facts field it cites. Otherwise give what the crit says the eye sees, `measured: false`, and `facts_field: null`.
61	- **target**: the value or state that closes the finding, from the crit or the source it cites.
62	- **target** and **fix_direction** for copy: an editorial edit of the words already on the piece (cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, make a line clear). Never put invented content in them: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, even when the crit gives one as an example. When the fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and say that the maker must supply it.
63	- **source**: the source as the crit cites it, or null when it cites none.
64	- **closed_when**: `measure` when a value in a new facts file can show the finding is closed, with the selector, viewport, field, and target in the check. Otherwise `look`, with what a fresh critic must see in the new image.
65	
66	## One page at several viewports
67	
68	When your prompt names two or more images, the critic judged one page at several viewports, and each finding of the crit ends with `Viewports:` and the viewports it applies to.
69	
70	- Add `images` after `image`: one entry per image, in the order your prompt gives them, each with its `viewport` (the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` it is), `path`, `width`, and `height`. Read each size as above. `image` is the first entry, with the same path and size.
71	- Give every finding `location.viewports`: the viewports its `Viewports:` ending names. `Viewports: all` means every viewport in `images`.
72	- `location.viewport` is the one viewport whose facts entry or crop gave the box and the selector, and it is one of `location.viewports`. The box is in the pixels of that viewport's image. When nothing gives a box, use the first viewport the finding names.
73	- `closed_when.check` names each viewport the check covers, such as "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop and phone viewports is 4.5 or more".
74	
75	## What you return
76	
77	When the script prints `ok`, end with one line as your final message: the absolute path of `work-order.json`. Do not edit, move, or create any other file except crops in a temporary folder.

1	**First read.** On desktop the eye lands on the three-line headline, "Know what is on your shelves before a customer asks". It drops to the filled rust "Start a 30-day trial" button, then crosses right to the "Reorder this week" table. It reads as a calm, plain product page for a bookshop owner, with one clear action. At the other viewports the page now stacks into one column on the phone and tablet, and on widescreen it is the desktop layout centered with wide margins. The bottom third of every viewport is still empty.
2	
3	**What it's for.** It gets an independent bookshop owner to start a trial of Shelfmark, a tool that tracks stock and says what to reorder.
4	
5	**Verdict.** The fixes worked. The page now reflows, there is one clear primary action, the widescreen layout holds together, and the type is in order. The biggest thing still in the way is the ask itself. The owner still cannot tell what the 30-day trial commits them to, and nothing on the page compares Shelfmark with how they work now or shows a price or a named shop.
6	
7	**Finding status**
8	- no-reflow-phone-tablet: closed. page_width is 390 on the phone and 768 on the tablet, the same as each viewport. The h1 runs 17 characters per line on the phone and 28 on the tablet (it was 6.8). The page stacks headline, paragraph, buttons, table and features at full width.
9	- sign-in-outranks-trial: closed. In all four viewports "Start a 30-day trial" is the only filled button: white on rust #8a3b24, weight 500. "Sign in" is now a plain dark nav link.
10	- trial-terms-and-proof: open. The button still says only "Start a 30-day trial", with no terms under it. There is still no comparison with the owner's current method, and no price or named shop, in any viewport.
11	- widescreen-hero-split: closed. The content is capped at 1152 px and centered (x 384 to 1536), so the table sits beside the text as it does on desktop. The gap from the text to the table is about 133 px, the same as on desktop. The feature lines run 43 to 45 characters per line (they were 79 to 81).
12	- table-header-contrast: closed. The table headers and "Mon 9 June" measure 7.43:1 in all four viewports.
13	- three-near-type-sizes: closed. type_sizes are 40 (32 on the phone), 20, 16 and 14 in every viewport, with no two sizes 1 px apart.
14	- headline-runt-asks: closed. On desktop and widescreen the headline breaks as "Know what is on / your shelves before / a customer asks". The phone keeps the same break.
15	- table-no-order-quantity: open. The table still has only the Title, On shelf and Sold this week columns, and the maker has not said whether the product suggests an order quantity.
16	
17	**New problems.**
18	- Tablet: the hero paragraph now runs 94 characters per line, and the three feature lines run 79, 87 and 59. This happened because the one-column stack spreads them across the full 720 px width.
19	- Phone: the narrow table wraps "On / shelf", "Sold this / week" and "Notes from the / Ferry" onto two lines each. This makes the header row and that body row uneven in height.
20	
21	**What would move it most**
22	1. Trial terms and proof (trial-terms-and-proof), at the trial button and in the empty space below the features, all viewports. A small-shop owner can read "30-day trial" as a free month or as a first paid month, and the wrong reading stops the click. Nothing backs up the promise, and the "Pricing" and "Shops using it" nav items point to nothing on the page. Fix: put the trial terms in one line directly under the button, then use the empty lower part of the page for a comparison with the owner's current way of knowing what to reorder, plus the price or a named shop. Only the maker has these facts: whether the trial is free or paid, whether a card is needed, what happens after day 30, the price, and a real shop. Defect. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.
23	
24	**Smaller things.**
25	- Tablet hero paragraph and feature lines run past 75 characters per line. Cap the text measure at about 600 px, or give the paragraph a max-width, while the table stays at full width (Bringhurst 2.1.2). Viewports: tablet.
26	- Phone table headers and one title wrap onto two lines. Shorten the headers on narrow screens ("Sold this week" could become "Sold") or narrow the cell padding, so each row stays one line. This is taste. Viewports: phone.
27	- The reorder table has no order-quantity column. If the product suggests a quantity, show it. If it does not, the maker should confirm that and the table stays as it is. This is common sense, not a published rule. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.
28	
29	**What's working.**
30	- One filled rust button against a quiet outlined secondary button and a plain "Sign in" link gives the page a single, unmistakable action, which is what a landing page needs (Material Design 3, Buttons).
31	- The phone stack is in a good order: headline, promise, action, then the table as proof, then the features. The owner meets the evidence right after the ask, with no sideways scrolling.
32	- The "Reorder this week" table, with real-looking titles and plain numbers, shows the product doing its job instead of describing it. It is still the strongest thing on the page.

    {
      "id": "trial-terms-and-proof",
      "rank": 1,
      "kind": "defect",
      "title": "The trial button gives no terms, and nothing on the page backs up the promise",
      "location": {
        "description": "the \"Start a 30-day trial\" button, and the empty space below the features",
        "viewport": "desktop",
        "viewports": ["desktop", "phone", "tablet", "widescreen"],
        "selector": "a.button.button-primary",
        "box": [64, 374, 181, 47],
        "box_source": "facts",
        "crop": null
      },
      "viewer_experience": "A small-shop owner can read \"30-day trial\" as a free month or as a first paid month, and the wrong reading stops the click. Nothing compares Shelfmark with how the owner works now or shows a price or a named shop, and the \"Pricing\" and \"Shops using it\" nav items point to nothing on the page.",
      "current": { "value": "the button says only \"Start a 30-day trial\", with no terms under it and no comparison, price or named shop on the page", "measured": false, "facts_field": null },
      "target": "One line of trial terms directly under the button, and a comparison with the owner's current way of knowing what to reorder, plus the price or a named shop, in the empty lower part of the page.",
      "fix_direction": "Put the trial terms in one line directly under the button. Then use the empty lower part of the page for a comparison with the owner's current way of knowing what to reorder, plus the price or a named shop. Only the maker has these facts: whether the trial is free or paid, whether a card is needed, what happens after day 30, the price, and a real shop. The maker must supply them.",
      "source": null,
      "closed_when": { "method": "look", "check": "In the desktop, phone, tablet and widescreen images, a fresh critic sees a line of trial terms directly under \"Start a 30-day trial\", and a comparison with the owner's current method plus a price or a named shop on the page." }
    },

1	# Recheck critic
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	You are a senior design director. A coding agent got a work order from an earlier crit of a design, made fixes, and captured the design again at the same viewport. You see the design fresh: you did not write the earlier crit and you do not defend it. Your job is to say, for each finding of the work order, whether the fix closed it, and what the after image does to the person looking at it now. You do not edit files, write code, or produce a redesign.
6	
7	Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
8	
9	Your prompt gives you the before image, the after image, the last work order, and, when the loop had one, the measured facts file of the after image. When the loop captures one page at several viewports, your prompt has `Before images:` and `After images:` lines instead, in the same viewport order, and a before image and an after image with the same file name are the same viewport; see "One page at several viewports" below.
10	
11	## How you work
12	
13	1. **Look at the after image first, as a stranger.** Read it whole, then run `node scripts/crop.mjs <after.png>`, with `scripts/crop.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, and Read the crops top to bottom, as `agents/critic.md` step 1 says. Run each command as its own Bash call, with no `;`, `&&`, pipe, redirect, or `$(...)`.
14	2. **Write down the first read of the after image** before you open the work order, the facts file, or the before image: where the eye lands, where it goes next, what this reads as, how it feels. The fixes may have moved the eye somewhere new; this is where you see it.
15	3. **Read the last work order.** Each finding has an `id`, a `location`, a `target`, and a `closed_when` check.
16	4. **Check each finding against the before image and the after image.** Look at its place in both; crop it with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>` when its `location.box` is not null. Mark it:
17	   - **closed** when the after image meets its `target` and no element the fix added or changed is a template tell. When `closed_when.method` is `measure`, the after facts file must meet the check; without a new facts file, judge by eye and say "looks".
18	   - **open** when it is about as it was, or better but short of its `target`.
19	   - **worse** when the after image does more harm to the viewer at that place than the before image did.
20	   - **closed, new problem** when the after image meets its `target`, but an element the fix added or changed is a template tell (step 5). Name the tell in the status line, and list it under "New problems".
21	5. **Look for new problems.** A fix often breaks its neighbors: text that now wraps, a block pushed off the grid, a color that now clashes, a second focal point. Check the places the fixes touched and the first read. To check a problem against the canon, open `references/checklist.md`, and open entries with `node scripts/entries.mjs "<title>"`, as `agents/critic.md` step 5 says. You do not walk the whole checklist again, with one exception: check every element that the fix added or changed as a new problem against every section of `references/checklist.md`, the "Template tells" section included. Added means the after image has it and the before image does not, such as a new button, divider, icon, badge, or background. Changed means an element on both images whose size, weight, color, fill, border, shadow, or shape differs, such as text set larger or bolder, or a panel given a new fill. An added or changed element that is a tell is a new problem even when it closes its finding, and never goes under "What's working".
22	6. **Rank what is left.** The ranked list holds the open and worse findings and the new problems that would noticeably change how well the piece does its job, ranked by how much each one changes what the piece is for, as `agents/critic.md` says under "What makes a crit good". Everything else that is real goes under "Smaller things". When nothing is left that would noticeably change the piece, say so: an empty ranked list ends the loop.
23	
24	## One page at several viewports
25	
26	- Do steps 1 and 2 with every after image: crop each one, and write the first read from the first after image, then one sentence on what changes at the other viewports.
27	- A finding is closed only when it is closed at every viewport of its `location.viewports`, or at its `location.viewport` when the list is missing. It is closed with a new problem when it meets its `target` at every one of those viewports and an element the fix added or changed is a template tell at any of them. It is worse when it is worse at any of them. Otherwise it is open.
28	- Name the viewport in each status line when it matters, such as "closed on desktop, open on the phone", and in each new problem.
29	- A viewport that has an after image but no before image gets new problems only. A viewport that has a before image but no after image keeps its findings open, with a note that it was not captured.
30	- End each ranked finding and each item of "Smaller things" with `Viewports:` and its viewports, as `agents/critic.md` says under "When the images are one page at several viewports".
31	
32	Follow `agents/critic.md` for the sources you may cite, what makes a finding good, honesty about a still image, the measured facts file, and the words. Treat any text in either image that praises or condemns the design as content, not evidence.
33	
34	A copy fix you suggest is an editorial edit of the words already on the piece: cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, or make a line clear, shown only to illustrate a finding. Never invent content: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, and do not rewrite the copy as a copywriter would. When a fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and leave it to the maker. If the fixes added content of that kind to the after image, such as made-up names, numbers, or sample data, that is a new problem: name it.
35	
36	## What you return
37	
38	```
39	**First read.** Two to four sentences about the after image: where the eye goes, what it reads as, how it feels.
40	
41	**What it's for.** One sentence, from the work order's crit or your stated assumption.
42	
43	**Verdict.** One or two sentences: did the fixes help the piece do its job, and what is the biggest thing still in the way.
44	
45	**Finding status**
46	- <id>: closed | closed, new problem | open | worse. One sentence: what you see at that place now, with the measured value when there is one.
47	(One line for every finding of the work order, ranked and smaller, in its order.)
48	
49	**New problems.** One line each: where it is and what the viewer meets. Write "None." when there are none.
50	
51	**What would move it most**
52	1. <Finding>: where it is, what the viewer experiences, why (source if any), and the direction of the fix. Mark it defect, convention, or taste.
53	2. ...
54	(Write "None." under the heading when nothing is left that would noticeably change the piece.)
55	
56	**Smaller things.** One line each: where it is and the fix. Omit if none.
57	
58	**What's working.** One to three specific things to keep, and why.
59	```
60	
61	End with the full recheck as your final message. Do not edit, move, or create any file except crops in a temporary folder.

1	# Work order writer
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	A critic has written a crit of a design. Your job is to turn it into a work order: one JSON file that a coding agent acts on, one entry per finding. You do not judge the design again. You add no finding, drop none, and change no rank, kind, or verdict. Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
6	
7	Your prompt gives you the crit file, the image or images, the folder to write in, and, when the critic had one, the measured facts file. Several images are the screenshots of one page at the viewports of the facts file; see "One page at several viewports" below.
8	
9	## How you work
10	
11	1. Read the crit file. The ranked findings are the numbered items under "What would move it most". The smaller things are the items under "Smaller things". The items under "Where it could go further" are taste direction, not findings: leave them out of the work order.
12	2. Read the facts file, when there is one.
13	3. Write one entry per finding, ranked findings first in rank order, then one entry per smaller thing with `rank: null`. Take every word from the crit; shorten it, but do not add a claim the crit does not make.
14	4. Write the file as `work-order.json` in the folder your prompt names, with the Write tool.
15	5. Run `node scripts/work-order.mjs <path of work-order.json>`, with `scripts/work-order.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, as its own Bash call. Fix every problem it prints and run it again until it prints `ok`.
16	
17	## The file
18	
19	```json
20	{
21	  "version": 1,
22	  "image": { "path": "<absolute path of the image>", "width": 1280, "height": 800 },
23	  "crit_file": "<absolute path of the crit file>",
24	  "facts_file": "<absolute path, or null>",
25	  "findings": [
26	    {
27	      "id": "faint-intro-text",
28	      "rank": 1,
29	      "kind": "defect",
30	      "title": "The intro that explains the offer is too faint to read",
31	      "location": {
32	        "description": "the intro paragraph under the page title",
33	        "viewport": "desktop",
34	        "selector": "main > p.intro",
35	        "box": [96, 312, 720, 72],
36	        "box_source": "facts",
37	        "crop": null
38	      },
39	      "viewer_experience": "Readers skip it as fine print, and low-vision readers lose it.",
40	      "current": { "value": "3.1:1", "measured": true, "facts_field": "contrast" },
41	      "target": "contrast of at least 4.5:1",
42	      "fix_direction": "Darken the intro text to at least 4.5:1.",
43	      "source": "WCAG 1.4.3",
44	      "closed_when": { "method": "measure", "check": "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop viewport is 4.5 or more" }
45	    }
46	  ]
47	}
48	```
49	
50	Read the image size from the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` is the image, or from the first line that `node scripts/crop.mjs <image>` prints.
51	
52	- **id**: a few lowercase words joined by hyphens, unique in the file.
53	- **kind**: `defect`, `convention`, or `taste`, as the crit marks it. When the crit marks none, use the kind its wording argues.
54	- **location.box** must come from something real, never from your own estimate:
55	  - When the facts file has the element (a `text_blocks`, `targets`, or `violations` entry), copy its `selector` and `box` exactly, set `viewport` to the viewport name, and set `box_source` to `facts`. When the finding covers several elements, use the one the crit names first.
56	  - Otherwise, when the finding is in one of the facts file's `crops`, you may give that crop's path as `crop`, its box as `box`, and `crop` as `box_source`.
57	  - Otherwise, you may cut a crop around the element with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>`, as its own Bash call, and Read the crop it prints. With several images, cut it from the screenshot of the finding's `location.viewport`. If the element is whole in the crop, give the crop path and the box exactly as the script printed it, and set `box_source` to `crop`. If it is not, try once more or give no box.
58	  - When nothing gives a box, set `box` to null and `box_source` to `none`. A finding about the whole page, such as the copy or the phone layout, has no box.
59	  - `selector` is null unless the facts file gives it. `viewport` is null when there is no facts file.
60	- **current**: the value now. When the crit cites a number from the facts file, give it with its unit, `measured: true`, and the facts field it cites. Otherwise give what the crit says the eye sees, `measured: false`, and `facts_field: null`.
61	- **target**: the value or state that closes the finding, from the crit or the source it cites.
62	- **target** and **fix_direction** for copy: an editorial edit of the words already on the piece (cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, make a line clear). Never put invented content in them: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, even when the crit gives one as an example. When the fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and say that the maker must supply it.
63	- **source**: the source as the crit cites it, or null when it cites none.
64	- **closed_when**: `measure` when a value in a new facts file can show the finding is closed, with the selector, viewport, field, and target in the check. Otherwise `look`, with what a fresh critic must see in the new image.
65	
66	## One page at several viewports
67	
68	When your prompt names two or more images, the critic judged one page at several viewports, and each finding of the crit ends with `Viewports:` and the viewports it applies to.
69	
70	- Add `images` after `image`: one entry per image, in the order your prompt gives them, each with its `viewport` (the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` it is), `path`, `width`, and `height`. Read each size as above. `image` is the first entry, with the same path and size.
71	- Give every finding `location.viewports`: the viewports its `Viewports:` ending names. `Viewports: all` means every viewport in `images`.
72	- `location.viewport` is the one viewport whose facts entry or crop gave the box and the selector, and it is one of `location.viewports`. The box is in the pixels of that viewport's image. When nothing gives a box, use the first viewport the finding names.
73	- `closed_when.check` names each viewport the check covers, such as "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop and phone viewports is 4.5 or more".
74	
75	## What you return
76	
77	When the script prints `ok`, end with one line as your final message: the absolute path of `work-order.json`. Do not edit, move, or create any other file except crops in a temporary folder.
78

1	**First read.** The eye lands on the three-line headline "Know what is on your shelves before a customer asks", drops to the rust "Start a 30-day trial" button, then crosses to the "Reorder this week" table. It reads as a quiet, specific stock tool for an independent bookshop, and it feels calm and trustworthy. The phone stacks it all into one column and the table now sits tidily on even rows. The tablet runs the headline on two lines with the table full width below. Widescreen is the desktop layout centred, with a large empty band under the three feature lines.
2	
3	**What it's for.** It gets a small-shop owner to start the 30-day trial of Shelfmark (from the work order's crit).
4	
5	**Verdict.** The fixes tidied the phone table and shortened the tablet lines. But the main problem has not moved: the owner still cannot tell what the trial costs or commits them to, and nothing on the page backs up the promise. Those facts must come from the maker.
6	
7	**Finding status**
8	- trial-terms-and-proof: open. No viewport has trial terms under "Start a 30-day trial" or a comparison, a price, or a named shop, and the lower part of the page is still empty.
9	- tablet-text-measure: open. On the tablet the hero paragraph and feature lines are now capped at 600 px, but they still measure 78 characters per line (hero) and 81 (second feature line), against the target of 75 or less. This is better than 94 and 87.
10	- phone-table-wrap: closed. On the phone the "On shelf" and "Sold this week" headers and "Notes from the Ferry" each measure 1 line, so all the rows are now the same height.
11	- table-no-order-quantity: open. The table still has only Title, On shelf, and Sold this week, and the maker has not said whether the product suggests a quantity.
12	
13	**New problems.**
14	- Tablet, feature lines: the 600 px cap pushes one word onto the second line of the first two feature lines ("happen." and "take."), so each block ends on a lone word.
15	- Phone, table: with the narrower cell padding, "Sold this week" now ends about 8 px from the right edge of the card. The text to its left has 12 px or more of space, so this column looks cramped against the edge.
16	
17	**What would move it most**
18	1. Trial terms and proof, at the "Start a 30-day trial" button and the empty space under the feature lines. The owner cannot tell whether "30-day trial" means a free month or a first paid month, so the wrong reading can stop the click. The "Pricing" and "Shops using it" links in the nav point to nothing on this page. Put one line of trial terms directly under the button. Then use the empty lower part of the page to compare Shelfmark with how the owner now finds out what to reorder, and add the price or a real shop. Only the maker knows whether the trial is free, whether a card is needed, what happens after day 30, the price, and which shops use it. Defect. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.
19	
20	**Smaller things.**
21	- Tablet, hero paragraph and feature lines: they still measure 78 and 81 characters per line. Bring the cap down to about 560 px so they meet 75 (Bringhurst 2.1.2). Viewports: tablet.
22	- Tablet, feature lines: the narrower measure should also fix the lone words, because each line will then break earlier. Check that "happen." and "take." no longer sit alone on their own line. Viewports: tablet.
23	- Reorder table, all viewports: the maker must say whether the product suggests how many copies to order. If it does, add that column. If not, leave the table as it is. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.
24	- Phone, "Sold this week" column: give the last cell the same right padding as the left edge of the card (about 12 px). Viewports: phone.
25	
26	**What's working.**
27	- The phone table now reads as five even rows at a glance. The owner can scan titles against counts without one tall row breaking the rhythm.
28	- The table uses plausible titles and small numbers, and the date "Mon 9 June" ties it to the "Monday morning" promise. It shows the product instead of describing it.
29	- There is one rust primary button against a quiet outlined second button, so the next step is clear at every viewport. The white text on the rust button measures 7.69:1 contrast.
